hints: Think about the two very different ways $\text{KMnO}_4$ can react with a C=C bond, one gentle that keeps the carbon skeleton intact and one vigorous that breaks it apart.
walkthrough:
Picture what happens to the double bond**
Imagine $\text{CH}_3\text{CH=CHCH}_3$. With gentle oxidation you simply add an $\text{-OH}$ to each carbon of the double bond and keep all four carbons joined together. With hot, concentrated, acidified oxidation you chop the molecule at the double bond to make acids or ketones.

Link conditions to product Y**
Later evidence shows $\mathbf{Y}$ still has four carbons joined in a chain and is not an acid, so the skeleton was not cleaved. That only happens under mild conditions, cold and dilute, often made alkaline.

hints: Use the two chemical tests to decide the functional group: no reaction with $\text{Na}_2\text{CO}_3$ rules out one acidic group, while gas with Na confirms another O-H containing group.
Convert the volume of gas to moles using $n = V/24000$ with V in $\text{cm}^3$ and compare moles of gas to moles of Y to find the reacting ratio.
Recall that each $\text{-OH}$ group gives only $\tfrac{1}{2}\text{H}_2$ with Na, so work out how many $\text{-OH}$ groups per molecule are needed to give the observed moles of $\text{H}_2$.
walkthrough:
Read the functional group clues**
No fizz with $\text{Na}_2\text{CO}_3$ tells you there is no $\text{-COOH}$ group, because acids release $\text{CO}_2$ with carbonate. Gas with excess Na tells you there is an $\text{-OH}$ group, because both alcohols and acids release $\text{H}_2$ with Na: $$2\text{R-OH} + 2\text{Na} \rightarrow 2\text{RONa} + \text{H}_2$$ So $\mathbf{Y}$ is an alcohol, not an acid.

Turn the gas volume into moles**
Convert carefully: $$n(\text{H}_2) = \frac{V}{24000} = \frac{24.0}{24000} = 0.001 \text{ mol}$$ You started with 0.001 mol of $\mathbf{Y}$. So the ratio is: $$0.001 \text{ mol Y} \rightarrow 0.001 \text{ mol H}_2$$ That is 1 mol $\text{H}_2$ per mol $\mathbf{Y}$.

Use the alcohol stoichiometry to count OH groups**
One $\text{-OH}$ gives only half a molecule of $\text{H}_2$: $$\text{R-OH} + \text{Na} \rightarrow \text{RONa} + \tfrac{1}{2}\text{H}_2$$ To get a whole $\text{H}_2$ per molecule, you need two $\text{-OH}$ groups per molecule. So $\mathbf{Y}$ is a diol.

Build the carbon skeleton**
But-2-ene is $\text{CH}_3\text{CH=CHCH}_3$, an unbranched 4C chain. Mild oxidation adds one $\text{-OH}$ to each carbon of the C=C without breaking the chain. That gives: $$\text{CH}_3\text{CH(OH)CH(OH)CH}_3$$ This is butane-2,3-diol, a possible structure for $\mathbf{Y}$.

Final answer: $\mathbf{Y}$ is $\text{CH}_3\text{CH(OH)CH(OH)CH}_3$, butane-2,3-diol.
$\mathbf{Y}$ does not react with $\text{Na}_2\text{CO}_3$ so is not a carboxylic acid, but gives gas with Na so contains $\text{-OH}$ groups.
$n(\text{H}_2) = 24.0/24000 = 0.001$ mol from 0.001 mol $\mathbf{Y}$. Since $\text{R-OH} + \text{Na} \rightarrow \text{RONa} + \tfrac{1}{2}\text{H}_2$, 1 mol $\mathbf{Y}$ gives 1 mol $\text{H}_2$, so $\mathbf{Y}$ contains two $\text{-OH}$ groups on an unbranched 4C chain from but-2-ene.

hints: Focus on the tiny peak at $m/e = 65$ (M+1) compared to the molecular ion at $m/e = 64$ and recall which isotope causes an M+1 peak in organic molecules.
walkthrough:
See why the small M+1 peak counts carbons**
Almost all carbon is $^{12}\text{C}$, but about 1.1% is $^{13}\text{C}$. A molecule with $n$ carbons has $n$ chances to contain one $^{13}\text{C}$, so the height of the M+1 peak relative to M grows with $n$: $$n(\text{C}) = \frac{\text{abundance M+1}}{\text{abundance M}} \times \frac{100}{1.1}$$

Substitute the values from Fig. 5.1**
Here M is at $m/e = 64$ with abundance 100, and M+1 is at $m/e = 65$ with abundance 2.2: $$n = \frac{2.2}{100} \times \frac{100}{1.1} = 2$$ So each molecule of $\mathbf{Z}$ contains 2 carbon atoms.

hints: Compare the heights of the peaks at $m/e = 64$ and $m/e = 66$ and think which halogen exists as two isotopes two mass units apart in an approximate 3:1 ratio.
walkthrough:
Spot the M+2 fingerprint**
The molecular ion M is at $m/e = 64$ with abundance 100. There is another peak two units higher at $m/e = 66$ with abundance 33.3. That M : M+2 pattern of about 3:1 is the classic signature of chlorine, because natural chlorine is about 75% $^{35}\text{Cl}$ and 25% $^{37}\text{Cl}$.

Assign the peaks**
Molecules containing $^{35}\text{Cl}$ appear at $m/e = 64$. The same molecules containing the heavier $^{37}\text{Cl}$ instead appear at $m/e = 66$. Bromine would give an almost 1:1 M : M+2 pattern, so it is ruled out.

Final answer: Chlorine, $\text{Cl}$. Ratio M : M+2 $= 100 : 33.3 \approx 3:1$, corresponding to $^{35}\text{Cl} : ^{37}\text{Cl}$, so peak at $m/e = 66$ is the molecular ion containing $^{37}\text{Cl}$.

hints: Start from what you already know: $\mathbf{Z}$ has 2 carbons and one Cl, with $M_r = 64$, so work out how many hydrogens must be present.
For $m/e = 29$, try combinations of C and H only that add to 29, remembering a fragment carries a + charge.
For $m/e = 49$, remember Cl can be 35 or 37, so use $^{35}\text{Cl}$ for the light fragment and see what C and H mass must be added to reach 49.
walkthrough:
Work out the full molecular formula first**
$M_r = 64$ from the molecular ion. Subtract 2 carbons $(24)$ and one $^{35}\text{Cl}$ $(35)$: $$64 - 24 - 35 = 5$$ So the formula is $\text{C}_2\text{H}_5\text{Cl}$, which is chloroethane. This helps you make sense of the fragments.

Assign the $m/e = 29$ fragment**
This mass is too low to contain Cl (mass 35). Try hydrocarbons: $2 \times 12 + 5 \times 1 = 29$. That fits perfectly: $$\text{C}_2\text{H}_5^{+}$$ This is the ethyl fragment formed by loss of Cl from the molecular ion.

Assign the $m/e = 49$ fragment**
Use the light chlorine isotope $^{35}\text{Cl}$: $$12 + (2 \times 1) + 35 = 49$$ That gives: $$\text{CH}_2\text{Cl}^{+}$$ This is the chloromethyl fragment formed by loss of a $\text{CH}_3$ group. Together the fragments confirm $\mathbf{Z}$ is $\text{CH}_3\text{CH}_2\text{Cl}$, chloroethane.
